query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing part of the FeCoNi lattice with Cr – forming an equiatomic FeCoNiCr high‐entropy alloy – will induce internal antiferromagnetic coupling and subtle chemical ordering that increases domain wall pinning, thereby enhancing the overall coercivity compared to the baseline FeCoNi-based soft magnets.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with an fcc single-phase structure that exhibits high saturation magnetization and low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Substitute one of the ferromagnetic components with Cr to form a nearly equiatomic FeCoNiCr alloy while maintaining high configurational entropy (≥1.0R) and processing conditions that stabilize the fcc structure.
generation.conditions: Synthesis should be performed under high-temperature processing conditions that produce a single-phase fcc structure with an almost equiatomic composition. The processing should avoid inducing significant phase separation or unwanted decomposition that could impair high saturation magnetization.
generation.structural_mediator: The introduction of Cr is expected to promote subtle chemical ordering or nanometer-scale phase modulation that results in enhanced domain wall pinning.
generation.mechanism: Cr, possessing antiferromagnetic characteristics, when incorporated into the ferromagnetic FeCoNi matrix, creates regions of antiferromagnetic coupling. This magnetic heterogeneity increases magnetic anisotropy and generates effective pinning centers for domain walls, thereby raising the coercivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in coercivity relative to the baseline FeCoNi alloy (and previously studied Pd- or Pt-containing derivatives) is anticipated, though it may be accompanied by a moderate reduction in saturation magnetization due to Cr's antiferromagnetic effects.
generation.baseline: FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys without Cr substitution, such as the soft magnetic FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt derivatives.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected provided that the alloy retains a stable fcc structure, maintains near-equiatomic composition, and is processed under conditions that prevent large-scale phase separation. Deviations in processing, or excessive Cr incorporation leading to a non-fcc structure, could nullify the expected enhancement.
generation.uncertainty: The precise increase in coercivity and the balance between enhanced hardening and potential loss in saturation magnetization remain to be experimentally quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of high-entropy alloys: one baseline equiatomic FeCoNi alloy and one modified equiatomic FeCoNiCr alloy under identical high-temperature processing conditions to stabilize a single-phase fcc structure. Characterize the phase structure using X-ray diffraction and measure the magnetic properties using SQUID magnetometry or VSM. Compare the coercivity and saturation magnetization of both samples.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (to confirm single-phase fcc structure)
SQUID or vibrating sample magnetometry measurements for coercivity (Hc)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coercivity of the FeCoNiCr alloy is not significantly higher (e.g., less than a 20% increase) than that of the baseline FeCoNi alloy, or if the introduction of Cr leads to unacceptable degradation of the fcc phase or magnetic performance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, we have achieved high magnetic anisotropy in rare‐earth‐free high entropy metallic thin films by sputtering and RTA. Robust magnetic order of both fcc FeCoNiMnCu and L10 (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt films has been demonstrated. The FeCoNiMnCu films exhibit a large coercivity increase after RTA, resulting from microstructural changes and strain‐induced anisotropy enhancement which strengthens domain wall pinning. Addition of Pt reduces the symmetry of the cubic fcc lattice to an intermetallic tetragonal L10 phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt. Although the Pt insertion lowers the configurational entropy compared to the equiatomic case, the entropy is still high enough to stabilize an L10 single phase. This intermetallic phase is confirmed to host high magnetocrystalline anisotropy, likely attributed to the lower symmetry of the L10 structure and the strong spin‐orbit coupling provided by the Pt insertion. These findings demonstrate the promise of high‐entropy intermetallic design as a key avenue to search for new high‐entropy magnets beyond the equiatomic composition.

The saturation magnetization of the AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi HEA reduces by more than 50% compared to samples with no Cr (AlCoFeNi). It has been previously reported earlier that MS falls linearly with increasing Cr content,,. This is mainly due to the antiferromagnetic nature of Cr. Additionally, the coercivity of the Cr containing alloy was higher than the alloy with no Cr. The MS and HC of AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi decreases with increasing annealing temperature. It has been previously reported that magnetic hardening of Fe–Co–Cr alloys is associated with the formation of a two-phase microstructure at the nanometer scale; firstly, the Fe–Co rich ferromagnetic phase, and secondly, the Cr rich antiferromagnetic phase. The relationship between the decomposition of the B2 phase into a two-phase B2 + BCC microstructure and the resulting coercivity is not well understood in these alloy systems and requires further detailed investigation.

frame.goal: To achieve an increased coercivity (i.e., a transition from soft to harder ferromagnetic behavior) in an almost equiatomic high-entropy alloy while maintaining a configurational entropy of at least 1.0R.
frame.limitation: Prior high-entropy alloy designs using Pd or Pt have not overcome soft ferromagnetism, remaining with low coercive fields.

decision.trend: Initial efforts to increase coercivity in FeCoNi‐based high-entropy alloys focused on heavy noble metal additions (Pd and Pt) to the base fcc structure, but those interventions maintained a soft magnetic state. In parallel, other studies on related HEAs (such as AlCoFeNi alloys) showed that replacing a ferromagnetic component (e.g., Co) with an element like Cr can trigger phase decomposition or induce ordering that increases coercivity. Thus, the trend has been from simple heavy-metal alloying—which did not deliver the desired hard magnetic behavior—to explorations of composition-induced electronic and structural modifications that can promote magnetic anisotropy.
decision.unsolved: How to achieve a single-phase, almost equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with an fcc structure that exhibits higher coercivity than that found in the Pd- or Pt-containing derivatives remains unresolved. In particular, a compositional intervention among 3d transition metals that can deliberately increase anisotropy or domain wall pinning, while preserving high saturation magnetization and configurational entropy, has not yet been explored.
decision.lever: Introduce Cr substitution into the FeCoNi matrix (i.e. design an equiatomic FeCoNiCr high-entropy alloy)
decision.why: Replacing part of the ferromagnetic elements with Cr is likely to introduce antiferromagnetic coupling and promote subtle phase transformations (or increased chemical ordering) that serve to pin magnetic domain walls, thereby increasing coercivity. This approach follows the trend observed in related systems (e.g., AlCoFeNi with Cr substitution) and directly addresses the limitation noted in the previous Pd/Pt derivatives while satisfying the composition and entropy constraints.
